title: The tangent-theta theorem
subtitle: Independent reading companion to G3 021000
adaptation: Edited G3 lecture prose restructured into readable slide units; formulas and selected SVG geometric models are authored companion material.

slides.title: The central problem
slides.lead: A trial subspace transverse to the exact orthogonal complement can be written as the graph of an operator from the exact subspace into its complement.
body: Its slope has singular values equal to the tangents of principal angles. We now show how a spectral gap controls that slope using a residual. The result is a single-angle tangent theorem. The proof has a similar outline to the sine theorem, but one essential extra step. We must prove that the trial space never points exactly into the unwanted complement. Otherwise the cosine has a kernel and the tangent cannot be recovered from finite graph coordinates.

slides.title: Fix the setting
slides.lead: Let A be a self-adjoint operator on a finite-dimensional real or complex inner-product space H.
body: Let U be an A-invariant subspace. Because A is self-adjoint, its orthogonal complement is also invariant. Let E be an isometry from a trial-coordinate space F into H. Write V for its range. Compress A to F to form the Ritz operator M, equal to E adjoint A E. Define the Ritz residual R by A E minus E M. Galerkin orthogonality says E adjoint R is zero.
slides.formula: δ‖tan Θ‖ ≤ ‖R‖ under an ordered Ritz gap

slides.title: Fix the setting · further detail
slides.lead: We assume the spectrum of M and the spectrum of A restricted to the unwanted complement are separated in an ordered way.
body: To fix an orientation, suppose every Ritz eigenvalue is at most alpha, while every complementary eigenvalue is at least alpha plus delta, for some positive delta. Reversing the order gives the analogous result.

slides.title: Fix the setting · continued
slides.lead: These are concrete hypotheses: they compare the computed Ritz spectrum with the exact unwanted spectrum, not merely the two blocks of A with one another.
body: The theorem says that delta times a unitarily invariant norm of the directed tangent is at most the same norm of the residual. It also proves the transversality needed for that tangent to represent actual principal angles.

slides.title: Why the ordered gap matters
body: C extracts the component of a trial vector inside U, and S extracts its component in U perpendicular. Since E is an isometry, the squared moduli satisfy cosine squared plus sine squared equals the identity on F. The source's coordinate tangent is S followed by the inverse of the positive cosine magnitude. In finite dimensions one can define a Moore–Penrose inverse even when the cosine is singular. But totalizing a formula does not make a ninety-degree angle finite. We need to establish that the cosine magnitude has no kernel.
slides.formula: ordered gap excludes intersection V ∩ U⊥

slides.title: Why the ordered gap matters · further detail
slides.lead: Suppose a nonzero trial vector E y lies entirely in U perpendicular.
body: Since A leaves U perpendicular invariant, its Rayleigh quotient is at least alpha plus delta. On the other hand, the same Rayleigh quotient equals the Rayleigh quotient of M at y, which is at most alpha, because M is the Ritz compression. Those two statements contradict one another. Therefore V has zero intersection with U perpendicular. This is the elementary transversality proof. In equal finite dimensions it also makes the horizontal projection invertible, so V is a graph over U. Without equal dimensions, the source uses a directed coordinate tangent rather than claiming an everywhere-defined graph over all of U.

slides.title: The residual equation is still present
slides.lead: Let F one be an isometric coordinate map onto U perpendicular, and let Lambda one represent A on that space.
body: Define X equal to F one adjoint E. Exactly as in the sine theorem, the complementary residual equation is Lambda one X minus X M equals F one adjoint R. An ordered spectral gap allows a constant-one Sylvester estimate on X. That immediately bounds the sine, since X has the same positive modulus as S. But the tangent is larger than the sine. Dividing by cosine without another argument would create an uncontrolled factor. Here is the decisive calculation for the operator norm.

slides.title: The residual equation is still present · further detail
slides.lead: Choose a unit trial-coordinate vector y that is a right singular vector of S.
body: Let its singular value be s, so the corresponding positive cosine magnitude is c, the square root of one minus s squared. Put v equal to the complementary component of E y.

slides.title: The residual equation is still present · continued
slides.lead: Then v has length s, and E adjoint v equals s squared times y.
body: Pair the residual R y with v. The unwanted block of A contributes at least alpha plus delta times s squared. The Ritz term contributes at most alpha times s squared. Therefore the real part of this pairing is at least delta times s squared. Now use Galerkin orthogonality: R y is perpendicular to the entire trial space. We may replace v in the inner product by its projection perpendicular to the trial space. The squared length of that projected vector is s squared minus s to the fourth power, so its length is s times c. If rho bounds the operator norm of R, Cauchy–Schwarz gives delta times s squared at most rho times s times c. For s positive, divide by s. We obtain delta times s at most rho times c.

slides.title: The residual equation is still present · continued
slides.lead: Since c is positive by transversality, divide again to obtain delta times tangent theta at most rho.
body: Choosing a largest singular value proves the operator-norm tangent estimate. Notice how the factor c appears from Galerkin orthogonality. Merely applying the earlier sine theorem would not have produced it. For the full unitarily invariant norm statement, the proof must control every leading singular-value sum. The finite-dimensional source supplies this through its ordered Ritz-gap theorem and its Ky Fan machinery. An operator-norm argument for only the largest singular value would not by itself prove the nuclear-norm or every other symmetric-gauge statement.

slides.title: Watch the theorem become equality in the plane
slides.lead: Take A diagonal with entries zero and five.
body: Let U be the horizontal axis, and take a trial unit vector with coordinates cosine theta and sine theta, where theta is strictly between zero and ninety degrees. The Ritz value M is five sine squared theta. The unwanted complementary eigenvalue is five. Therefore the actual ordered gap is five cosine squared theta. Apply A to the trial vector. Subtract the Ritz value times the same vector. The resulting Ritz residual is five sine theta cosine theta times a unit vector perpendicular to the trial line. Its length is five sine theta cosine theta.
slides.formula: δ sin θ ≤ ρ cos θ

slides.title: Watch the theorem become equality in the plane · further detail
slides.lead: The directed tangent is tangent theta.
body: Multiply it by the gap: five cosine squared theta times tangent theta equals five sine theta cosine theta. That is exactly the residual length. So the inequality is equality for every acute theta.

slides.title: Watch the theorem become equality in the plane · continued
slides.lead: This is a sharpness example, with the correct Ritz gap and the correct Ritz residual used consistently.
body: Notice the difference from the sine theorem's earlier example. There we fixed the trial operator at zero, and the residual had norm five sine theta. Here the Ritz operator follows the trial line, so both the residual and the relevant gap change with theta.

slides.title: The behavior near a right angle
slides.lead: As theta approaches ninety degrees, the tangent tends to infinity.
body: Does that contradict a bounded residual? No. In our example the Ritz eigenvalue approaches five, the unwanted eigenvalue. Thus the ordered gap tends to zero at the same time. The theorem's product remains equal to the residual. We cannot hold the old gap of five fixed while allowing the Ritz value to move toward five. This also explains why a uniform positive ordered gap implies transversality. If the cosine vanished in any direction, the corresponding Ritz quotient would enter the unwanted spectral region. The gap excludes that possibility. The tangent theorem therefore provides a stronger geometric conclusion than a sine bound, but only under a more structured comparison involving the Ritz spectrum.
slides.formula: δ tan θ = ‖R‖ in the planar Ritz example

slides.title: Operator norms, Frobenius norms, and arbitrary gauges
slides.lead: In operator norm, the result controls the worst principal slope.
body: If the largest tangent is at most rho divided by delta, every principal angle is at most the arctangent of rho over delta. This angle bound remains strictly below ninety degrees for every finite rho. In Frobenius norm, the squares of all directed tangents add. The theorem limits the aggregate squared slope by the squared residual length after scaling by delta. For a Ky Fan norm, the estimate bounds the sum of the largest several tangent singular values. General unitarily invariant norms then follow from the symmetric-gauge framework established. The source's exact theorem assumes an isometric trial frame and the Ritz identity. More general trial frames can be normalized, but the normalization and their lower bounds must be stated, rather than simply reusing the isometric formula.
slides.formula: tan θ grows when cos θ approaches zero

slides.title: What this theorem does not say
slides.lead: It does not state that arbitrary pairwise-separated spectra supply the same constant-one estimate in every norm.
body: It does not identify the graph of V over all of U when the dimensions do not match. And it does not allow a zero cosine to be treated as an ordinary finite tangent just because a Moore–Penrose inverse exists. Doubled-angle bounds instead arise from reflection identities and different spectral-gap configurations. Their conclusions cannot be substituted for the directed tangent estimate without checking the corresponding branch and norm hypotheses.
slides.takeaway: The tangent theorem uses an ordered Ritz gap to establish both transversality and a slope bound.
